item.title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
item.description:
There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders.

A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage.

The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies, enterprises should still be concerned.

“Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.”

Sophisticated tradecraft

ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk.

The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part.

Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained. 

“This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote.

They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual.

The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said.

The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla.

Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected

Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode.

“ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic.

“Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said.

This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted.

Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory.

Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said.

A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)  and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy.

Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said.

His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process.

But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described.

“A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.”

‘A level above’

And, said David Shipley, CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.”

Running on premises Exchange has been increasingly risky for years, he noted. For government, AI firms, finance, and other high-value targets, the risk of hosting on prem instead of using cloud-based versions continues to grow.

However, it’s worth noting that just having Microsoft host Exchange doesn’t mean you’re safe from nation-states, Shipley said. “It just raises the bar.” Another key challenge with Exchange servers is Microsoft’s own advice not to have anti-virus scanners looking in certain places like ExchangeTransport.exe, because doing so could create instability.

“They basically told criminals where to hide and why it’s good to hide there,” he noted. “Not that they can do much about it, but it points to a huge Catch-22.”

Another Catch-22: With the publication of this report and new ideas that will undoubtedly come from it, “we’ll likely see criminal groups consider the value of this kind of technique in the future,” Shipley noted.

item.title: What will it take to make VulnOps a reality?
item.description:
Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.”

VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks.

Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea.

The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries.

As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.”

Not your father’s vulnerability management program

The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.”

Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities.

They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices.

“The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tells CSO. “We’re now taking that into vulnerability management. If you think about what was different about DevOps, it was the philosophy about going from an iterative cycle to a continuous cycle with fast failure and feedback loops.”

Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, argues that AI must become central to how vulnerability management operates. “What we’re talking about here is an AI-centric workflow where the AI is doing most of the analysis, and humans are just overseeing the operation,” Skoudis tells CSO.

Not everyone, however, is convinced that VulnOps represents such a fundamental departure from established practices.

“It feels like a rebranding to me,” Chris Elgee, SANS principal instructor and senior security analyst at Counter Hack Challenges, tells CSO.

“Organizations have always had to deal with vulnerability management,” says Elgee, who agrees that the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery is putting new pressure on organizations, but questions whether VulnOps constitutes a fundamentally different discipline.

Is human-in-the-loop dead?

Experts disagree on one fundamental aspect of VulnOps as they currently understand the concept. The disagreement centers on how much human control can survive when vulnerability remediation has to operate at AI speed.

“The biggest struggle people have with patching vulnerabilities in general is that it’s disruptive to the workflows,” Ali Khan, CISO of AI-powered device security company Iru, tells CSO. “Generally, when there’s a security vulnerability and you need to patch it, you have to upgrade your source code or the third-party supply packages,” Khan explains.

“And generally, that leads to breaking changes, especially in legacy systems that have been long-lived and are in maintenance mode,” Khan says. “You don’t want to bring a company down or destroy their revenue stream by pushing a patch that essentially stops the business process.”

That risk is why most security professionals aren’t eager to take humans out of the loop.

CSA’s Mogull cautions, “We’re nowhere near fully automating [the remediation] part of the process. Eventually, we will need more, but we’re not there yet, even with today’s tools,” he says.

Nor does he envision VulnOps operating without human oversight. “Remember, humans are the ones that are accountable,” Mogull says. He points out that under the CSA operating model he helped develop, AI can make decisions within predefined policies, but potentially disruptive changes still require human intervention.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis argues for what he calls a governance-in-the-loop process where “you have governance that decides that, ‘Hey, if a given action that I take could fall below this governance-in-the-loop level, just do it. Automate it. Don’t even think about it.’”

“Each organization is going to have its own separate line for where governance in the loop will apply, but you could say, for example, regarding important patches for Windows workstations, deploy them if they’re critical, on a rolling basis. So, in other words, do 25% per hour or two, over the space of half a day.”

Knostic’s Evron, however, believes that even these arrangements may prove unsustainable as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“One of the main understandings of the last couple of months is that human in the loop is dead,” he says. “We simply can’t move fast enough for the vast majority of operations to have a human in the loop.”

On top of that, Evron questions whether autonomous patching itself will remain an adequate solution. “We must understand that patching is just not going to be fast enough,” Evron says. “We must start considering how we build security programs in a world where patching is not viable.”

Autonomous patching may only be transitional

Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove inadequate as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“Start your program for autonomous patching today, but understand that we need to prepare for a world without patching,” he warns. “If we have a human in the loop, it’s just a performer. The human would have all the responsibility with no authority and no ability to understand and comprehend what they’re doing.”

Evron argues that the industry should stop thinking exclusively about finding flaws and fixing them after the fact and should opt instead for software and defensive systems that prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced, detect and neutralize exploitation in the first place, or make individual vulnerabilities less consequential.

He sees three approaches to making these preventative systems a reality. The first is to embed them directly into AI coding agents, rather than relying primarily on vulnerability scanning after code has been written. “Control your coding agents and you control your code, so the code itself gets generated more secure,” Evron says. He also advocates scanning code for vulnerabilities upon generation, rather than waiting for it to enter traditional continuous integration pipelines.

The second approach is to detect and neutralize attacks at runtime. Evron describes what he calls “patch in place during runtime.” At this year’s [un]prompted conference, Evron went on stage to show ways of conducting patch in place during runtime. “As an attack is going on, it is detected in the logs and patched,” Evron says.

The third approach to creating a system that obviates the current patching cycle is to make patching less urgent through defense in depth, according to Evron. He suggests moving toward approaches in which critical vulnerabilities become a matter of defense in depth, “so you don’t necessarily need to patch immediately.”

Steps CISOs should be taking now

According to Evron, the most critical step CISOs should take in embracing VulnOps is to stop relying solely on established practices that may prevent them from recognizing how AI is fundamentally changing the threat environment.

For example, basic security hygiene remains important but cannot be treated as a sufficient response to AI-driven vulnerability discovery, he says. “Stop being afraid to imagine, go bigger, and understand that, well, of course our basics always matter; they will not save us,” he adds.

And yet other experts question how organizations can embrace the challenging new world of VulnOps without first nailing down their security basics. Counter Hack’s Elgee says, “A lot of organizations, maybe most organizations, don’t even have a full concept of what their entire asset inventory is.”

Iru’s Khan says that CISOs should start to think about how security and engineering need to renegotiate their relationships, given that security teams cannot simply hand developers remediation tickets and expect faster results. “This wall has to come down, and there has to be comfort letting other teams contribute in a technical way to systems,” Khan says.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis advises CISOs to begin implementing VulnOps without attempting to transform the entire enterprise over to a new paradigm. He argues that organizations should start to establish governance boundaries within which AI agents can operate.

“If it’s above the threshold, if it’s higher business risk, then you have to have a human review it,” Skoudis says. “But if it’s below the governance-in-the-loop threshold, push it.”

Evron is confident that CISOs can expect their existing teams to handle the transition to VulnOps, particularly if they reduce their dependence on the vulnerability scanning tools that kick out so many vulnerability reports. “The existing teams can handle this, but not with the current technologies they use,” he says. “We must stop paying mindlessly to the big scanning services because the bottleneck has always been fixing and patching.”

He adds, “Therefore, building a system where we trust autonomous patching is what we must do right now, in the immediate term, and longer term in our plans we must understand we will not be able to rely on patching.”

item.title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 63 Critical Microsoft fixes, plus an Outlook zero day that allows theft of hashed credentials
item.description:
A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases.

Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing.

Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed.

Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password. 

Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang, senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.”

Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network.

Microsoft patches

Of the 1,094 Microsoft vulnerabilities, 63 were rated as critical.

Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. The Windows LDAP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119958) lets an unauthenticated attacker run code inside the Windows LDAP service, which puts domain controllers and the whole Active Directory environment at risk.

The Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-118207) can be triggered by anyone able to send email to the organization, Bicer said, and the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-112967) gives an attacker on the same network full control of a Windows system.

The fourth, the Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119990), sits in a cloud service many teams now depend on. However, this service is automatically patched by Microsoft.  

Patch order should follow reach, not product names, Bicer advised CSOs. Domain controllers and Exchange servers go first, he said, followed by anything that exposes IIS, Microsoft Secure Channel (Schannel) or RPC to untrusted networks.

Message Queuing deserves an inventory before it gets a patch: find every server where the service is enabled, turn it off where no application needs it, and patch the rest the same day, he said, adding that hypervisor hosts need their own maintenance window, because one escaped guest becomes a problem for every tenant on that host.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action,” said Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative. That means first patching Exchange and domain controllers (meaning LDAP/Kerberos) to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on cloud services your organization uses.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, observed that there are fewer Microsoft vulnerabilities this month than there were in October, but noted, “I’m not foolish enough to think that this single drop indicates that we’re into the downward trend that I predicted we’ll see in the coming months. Instead, I think that we’re seeing a continuation of the elevated numbers as Microsoft continues to fix long hidden issues that are being surfaced by AI. Soon, however, these numbers will begin to decline as the last of these long-hidden issues are resolved and we only have new bugs to deal with.”

CSOs can help their teams by ignoring any noise coming from vendors and any vulnerabilities that are overhyped, Reguly said. When vulnerability counts started to rise, it was C-level employees who jumped up the fastest and added to the burden their admins were facing. “Now it’s time to settle down and support your teams rather than increasing their burden. CSOs should keep in mind that AI companies and security vendors may needlessly hype unimportant vulnerabilities because it is cheap, effective marketing for their services,” he pointed out. “A vulnerability isn’t critical if you don’t have the impacted software deployed.”

Prevention is key, so CSOs should focus their efforts on system hardening and mitigation. This, he said, will be more effective than chasing vulnerabilities. Finally, Reguly reminded CSOs that prioritization matters. “If you’ve developed a prioritization strategy that works for you, don’t change your process just because the media is looking for clicks,” he said.

SAP patches

The critical vulnerabilities collectively known as ICM2Shell are CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126. Researchers at Onapsis, who discovered them, said exploitation isn’t theoretical; they provided SAP with a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested.

To access the flaw, an attacker only needs network access to the HTTP/HTTPS port, says Onapsis. Because WebSocket support is enabled by default in both the ICM and the SAP Web Dispatcher, a system is exposed even if no application uses WebSocket. Some services, including default ICF services in SAP S/4HANA, accept WebSocket connections without authentication, and in others the flaw can be reached before authentication takes place. “Nothing in the chain requires an SAP user, a password or a certificate,” the researchers said.

The adm account owns the SAP installation, the researchers pointed out, including its executables, its instance profiles, its secure store, and its connection to the database. Running commands as that user grants full control of the SAP system. An attacker could, among other things recover database credentials and other secrets from the secure store and profiles and use them to read or alter any business data directly in the database; collect RFC destinations and technical credentials that let them move on to the SAP and non-SAP systems connected to this one; change configuration or binaries to keep persistent access; and destroy data.

Other patches

Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti, drew attention to patches from Adobe, Mozilla and Google.

Adobe released nine security bulletins that resolve 110 CVEs, 22 of which are critical. Adobe said it is not aware of any exploits in the wild. The two Priority 2 updates carry the most risk; Connect (APSB26-191) has the largest count at 24 CVEs, 18 of them critical and six rated CVSS 10.0. The vulnerabilities span SSRF, path traversal and SQL injection, and affect Windows on-prem versions 12.12 and earlier. The Experience Manager (APSB26-189) patch fixes 14 CVEs, including four Critical code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.9.

Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50, released on Monday, resolved nine CVEs including CVE-2026-125350, which is being actively exploited in the wild. This marks Chrome’s eighth zero-day exploit of 2026, Goettl noted. Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge will need the fix as well, and users should relaunch after updating for the patch to take effect. This patched release follows Chrome 157’s November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical. Separately, Google’s November Android bulletin fixed 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them critical, with none marked as exploited. The target is patch level is 2026-11-05 or later.

Mozilla’s November 10 release includes Firefox 160, which resolves 99 CVEs (57 of them are ranked High). Firefox ESR 153.7 resolves 81 vulnerabilities. (51 High), and ESR 115.45 resolves 28, all High. Many of the High-rated issues are use-after-free and memory boundary flaws across graphics, DOM, layout, and JavaScript components, including a number of sandbox escapes such as CVE-2026-124907, a use-after-free in CanvasWebGL that allows privilege escalation and sandbox escape. The same flaw is addressed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.
